title: Nofollow Links
description: The history and modern SEO nuance of rel="nofollow", sponsored, and ugc links.
subject: html
html:
rel="nofollow" tells search engines "don't pass ranking credit through this link" — originally created to fight comment-spam, it's now one of several precise relationship signals a site can send.

Syntax

<a href="https://untrusted-site.com" rel="nofollow">link text</a>

Basic Example

<p>Comment from a visitor: check out <a href="https://random-blog.com" rel="nofollow">my blog</a>!</p>

Browser output: visually identical to any other link — nofollow is invisible to a normal visitor and only matters to search engine crawlers.

Why nofollow Was Created

In the mid-2000s, spammers flooded blog comments with links purely to manipulate search rankings through sheer link volume. rel="nofollow" gave site owners a way to accept user comments without those links counting as an endorsement in the eyes of search engines.

Important Attributes / Related Values

ValueWhen to use it instead
nofollowGeneral "don't vouch for this" — untrusted or unreviewed links
sponsoredSpecifically for paid links, advertisements, or affiliate placements
ugcSpecifically for content submitted by users — comments, forum posts

Real-World Example

<p>This post is sponsored by our partner. <a href="https://partner.com" rel="sponsored noopener" target="_blank">Visit their site</a>.</p>

A disclosed sponsored link — using the more precise sponsored value rather than a generic nofollow, which is both more accurate and, in some regions, closer to what advertising disclosure regulations expect.

Common Mistakes

  • Applying a blanket nofollow meta tag to an entire page (blocking all links from passing credit) when only specific links actually need it
  • Using nofollow on genuinely trustworthy internal or editorial links out of over-caution
  • Using generic nofollow for paid or user-generated links instead of the more precise, honest sponsored/ugc values

Best Practices

  • Apply nofollow (or the more specific sponsored/ugc) only to the individual links that actually need it
  • Be transparent about paid placements — both for user trust and, in many jurisdictions, legal disclosure requirements

Accessibility Considerations

No effect on assistive technology — this is purely a crawler-facing signal.

SEO Considerations

Since Google's 2019 policy update, nofollow, sponsored, and ugc are all treated as hints rather than strict directives — meaning search engines may still choose to crawl and, in aggregate signal terms, weigh such links in some cases. This nuance doesn't remove the value of using the correct, honest attribute; it just means "nofollow" is no longer an absolute guarantee of zero influence.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

No visual or functional browser behavior changes — nofollow and its siblings are entirely a signal to automated crawlers, invisible in the rendered page.

Mini Practice

  1. Add rel="nofollow" to a link from an imagined public comment form.
  2. Rewrite that same example using the more precise ugc value instead, and explain why it's more accurate.
